front.title: web-stream: A General Purpose Message Framing over Byte-Stream Oriented Wire Protocols

abstract.t: This document defines a general-purpose message framing named web-stream, which supports message-based communication over any byte-stream oriented L7 protocols, in particular HTTP (as in its standard semantics ).
web-stream can be viewed as a binary alternative to the framing defined for the server-sent events (SSE) . This was the original goal when the initial version of the proposal was published in 2017.
For the rest of the document, we will use the term WiSH (i.e. Web in Strict HTTP) to refer to the core use case behind this proposal, and web-stream to refer to the web-stream framing format.

section.name: Background
section.t: There have been several attempts to improve message-based streaming communication on the Web.

The server-sent events (SSE) realized message-based streaming communication in the server-to-client direction. It introduced a new Web API and a special message framing format while using HTTP as the wire protocol.

WebSockets realized native client-server full-duplex message-based communication for the Web by introducing both a new Web API and a new wire protocol (the WebSocket Protocol). It has been implemented and deployed widely, but the wire protocol is not compatible with the broad HTTP ecosystem . Intermediaries and frameworks have to be upgraded to understand the wire protocol to support WebSockets.
This Internet-Draft addresses the aforementioned problem space with a solution fully compliant with standard HTTP semantics, informally referred to as Web in Strict HTTP (WiSH).

section.name: Introduction
section.t: web-stream offers a general-purpose message framing for use over the standard HTTP semantics to provide full-duplex messaging semantics. The framing is compatible with the well-adopted and security-proven base framing of the WebSocket Protocol . The underlying communication protocols providing the standard HTTP semantics can be HTTP/1.1 , HTTP/2 , HTTP/3 , or any future protocols. The web-stream framing can also be used over any other byte-stream oriented L7 protocols (over TCP or QUIC ).
Transport protocol features such as multiplexing and session priority are provided by the underlying L4 protocol .

HTTP implementations may not allow earlier 2xx responses , especially when HTTP/1.1 is used as the underlying transport. In such cases, parallel HTTP requests may be used to support full-duplex messaging between the client and server. Separately, when HTTP body streaming is unsupported by the Web client or blocked by intermediaries, multiple short-lived HTTP requests may be used to send messages between the client and server.

web-stream complies with the HTTP semantics (as opposed to turning it to a transport protocol). Consequently, while it utilizes the base framing of the WebSocket Protocol, it drops the opening handshake and the closing handshake.

section.name: Conformance Requirements and Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in .

Requirements phrased in the imperative as part of algorithms (such as "strip any leading space characters" or "return false and abort these steps") are to be interpreted with the meaning of the key word ("MUST", "SHOULD", "MAY", etc.) used in introducing the algorithm.
Conformance requirements phrased as algorithms or specific steps can be implemented in any manner, so long as the end result is equivalent.
In particular, the algorithms defined in this specification are intended to be easy to understand and are not intended to be performant.

section.name: Web-Stream over HTTP
section.t: This section describes how to use web-stream over the HTTP semantics .
To use web-stream for an HTTP request message or HTTP response message, the content part (aka body part) MUST be a sequence of zero or more web-stream frames defined in Section XXX.
The Content-Type header for an HTTP message using web-stream MUST be set to the web-stream media type, application/web-stream, which includes an optional message parameter.
Example:
The message parameter specifies the content type and encoding of the data exchanged within the payload of the web-stream messages.
The standard HTTP (REST) semantics should be followed, particularly regarding the choice of the HTTP method.
Some HTTP semantics, such as the Cache-Control header, may not be applicable when the HTTP body is streamed. However, such a limitation is not specific to web-stream.

section.name: Framing
section.t: The web-stream framing is largely compatible with the base framing protocol of the WebSocket Protocol , though some fields are used differently from the WebSocket Protocol.
A high-level overview of the framing is provided in the figure below.

section.name: Payload length
section.t: The payload length and extended payload length fields are used to determine the length of the Payload Data field of the frame, following the exact mechanism used in the WebSocket Protocol.

section.name: Fragmentation
section.t: The FIN bit and the continuation frame opcode enable a fragmentation mechanism, which is identical to that of the WebSocket Protocol. One or more continuous frames represent a web-stream message. The FIN bit indicates that the frame is the final frame of a web-stream message. For the second and following frames of a web-stream message, the opcode field MUST be set to the continuation frame opcode.
The mechanism allows for sending portions of a web-stream message with a large payload before the total size of the message is known.

section.name: Payload Compression
section.t: web-stream defines the CMP bit as the second most significant bit of the first octet of a frame. The CMP bit in the first frame of a message indicates whether that message's payload is compressed. When the message payload is compressed, the CMP bit of the first frame MUST be set to 1; otherwise, it MUST be set to 0. The CMP bit MUST always be set to 0 for all non-first frames. See Section XXX for details of the payload compression.

section.name: Opcode
section.t: For the "opcode" field, web-stream uses the following opcodes:

list.t: %x1 denotes the first frame of a text message
%x2 denotes the first frame of a binary message
%x3 denotes the first frame of a metadata message

section.t: Any values not listed above are reserved.
The continuation frame, text message, and binary message opcode retain the same meaning as the WebSocket Protocol.

web-stream introduces the metadata message opcode (%x3), which is used for exchanging metadata. When the opcode field of the first frame is set to %x3, the message contains metadata. The application-level protocol determines the encoding of the payload of metadata messages. Support for metadata is optional; web-stream implementations that do not support or consume metadata messages MAY discard them. The WebSocket Protocol's connection close frame opcode (%x8) is dropped for web-stream. The ping (%x9) and pong (%xA) control frames are retained from the WebSocket Protocol. web-stream endpoints MAY alternatively rely on keep-alive mechanisms provided by the underlying transport.

section.name: General Guidelines about Compression
section.t: For short-lived streaming, the content codings (aka HTTP body compression) MAY be applied in the underlying HTTP semantics layer for web-stream as specified in Section 8.4. Content-Encoding of . This is transparent to the web-stream framing and should perform well for short-lived streaming.

For long-lived streaming, some compression mechanisms like Per-message Compression for WebSocket (PMCE) may provide better performance. Standardization of such a mechanism with web--stream is planned for the future. For now, experimental implementations may port PMCE to web-stream as described in this section. We call this web-stream compression.

It's RECOMMENDED that web-stream implementations coordinate with the underlying HTTP semantics layer to decide whether to enable the web-stream compression. Only either of the web-stream compression or content coding should be enabled to avoid double compressing data.

section.name: web-stream Compression
section.t: defined a general framework on how to implement a message-oriented compression for using its extension framework. This is named Per-message Compression for WebSocket (PMCE). The web-stream compression is an adaptation (port) of PMCE for web-stream.

section.t: Enabling the web-stream compression requires the participating endpoints to perform the extension negotiation defined in through the headers of the HTTP request message and HTTP response message of the underlying HTTP semantics layer. section.name: Framing
section.t: web-stream compression uses the second significant bit of the first octet of a frame to indicate whether the message payload is compressed. It's named "Per-Message Compressed" bit in the PMCE specification. In the web-stream framing, this bit is named the CMP bit.
When the CMP bit is set on the first frame of a message, the message payload MUST be compressed.

section.name: Compression Methods other than DEFLATE
section.t: In addition to DEFLATE, web-stream compression variants for other compression algorithms such as Zstandard can be defined.

section.name: UTF-8 Requirements
section.t: The WebSocket Protocol requires endpoints to _Fail the WebSocket Connection_ when they encounter an invalid UTF-8 byte stream in a text message. Consequently, server frameworks typically check for UTF-8 validity.

In contrast, the contents of web-stream text messages also MUST be a valid UTF-8 stream, but web-stream endpoints are not REQUIRED to perform UTF-8 validation. This omission offers greater flexibility to server development, for example, a server may opt to perform the UTF-8 validity check within a JSON parser.
